title: Who is Elara Voss? (Max Read, 7 Aug 2025)
rule: Default LLM character names ('promptonyms') are a measurable tell across GPT, Claude, Gemini, LLaMA, DeepSeek and Grok. Never take the first name a model offers; blacklist the family (Elara/Elena/Elias + Voss/Vex/Vance/Thorne/Finch/Solis/Dorne) and the place-words Erebus, Eldora, Whispering Woods. Pick names by a rule, not by asking for 'a name'.
example: No person or book named Elara Voss before Aug 2023; 62 Amazon books credited to her; a Reddit test found Gemma used 'Elara' 39 times in 3 stories and 'Elias' 29 times in 4. Recurring: Elena Vex, Elara Vex, Elias Vance, Aris Thorne, Elara Finch, Elara Solis, Elara Dorne.

title: AI-generated baby name 'rolls off the tongue' (search summary; Laura Wattenberg quoted)
rule: Why defaults arrive: a blank name carries no baggage, and models are trained to please. A name that feels neutral to a model is the generic one; a name needs baggage (a place, a trade, a history) to belong to a world.
example: Wattenberg: 'The AIs love to create characters named Elara'; 'none of us have ever actually met a person named Elara, it has no baggage.' Named Elara 2025 Name of the Year.

title: The (Unspoken) Names, or Build a Fantasy Naming Language in One Afternoon
rule: Conlang-lite per culture: (1) pick a small consonant set, (2) pick the vowels you like, (3) fix a syllable template with C/V and optional slots, (4) allow only easy clusters, (5) one spelling per sound, then generate by hand or tool. Each culture gets its own tiny phonology, so its names look related. Also decide whether names mark gender, status or family.
example: C = p t k m n r, V = a i; template CV(C) yields ta, nik, ri, nam; clusters stop+r or nasal+unvoiced stop; 'umber' works better than 'umder'. Spelling choice per language: c for Oshaarun, k for Tlaanthothei, q for Qarsazhi.

title: The Language Construction Kit (Rosenfelder) book page
rule: Rosenfelder's LCK has a chapter on a 'naming language': a small language built only to name characters and map places. Method detail not retrieved from the page (chapter text not read).
example: 'How to create simple languages for naming characters and creating maps.' Zompist forum advice (search summary, unverified here): list a syllable type more than once to weight it.

title: What's In A Name (Ty Arthur, Goodreads author blog)
rule: Derive names from a character's core trait via real languages (Swedish, Icelandic, Albanian) so they sound foreign but not absurd; keep each region's names in one style (short and clipped for one city); avoid unpronounceable names and avoid both Richard-ordinary and Blipdoolpoolp-absurd.
example: Tala = Swedish/Icelandic 'to speak'; Myrr from Swedish 'myr' (mire); Erret = Albanian 'dusk'.

title: Situ design brief (place-name generator)
read: full (via fetch summarizer; a design brief, features planned)
rule: Place names are specific + generic elements, where the generic is a landscape term (peak, vale, ford, ham, ton). Tag elements by terrain (mountain, coast), give each culture its own composition syntax (Germanic compounds vs French linking particles), allow layered etymologies (several languages for one feature), and let forms erode (-ton/-tun). Names then read as accreted history.
example: Southampton = south + ham + ton; Swansea = 'Sven's island'; Noisy-le-Sec, Aix-la-Chapelle. Writing advice from the search: 'The Three Peaks' beats 'Mountain Kingdom'.

title: Generic Terms Australia (toponymy: specific vs generic elements)
rule: Toponymy treats a place name as specific + generic element; the generic names the kind of land, so even an opaque specific tells a reader what the place is. In very old names the generic's meaning has been lost, so some names should carry an unexplained generic.
example: Mount Kosciuszko, Botany Bay, Point Lookout (a generic acting as the specific).

title: Tolkien, On Fairy-Stories: secondary belief (journal article, via search summary)
rule: Tolkien's test: a secondary world is believed while the reader is 'inside' it because it accords with its own laws (inner consistency of reality); consistency gets harder the further the world departs from the primary one; the moment disbelief arises the spell breaks.
example: Tolkien (quoted in Mirante via gwern.net fetch): 'The moment disbelief arises, the spell is broken; the magic, or rather art, has failed.' and the world is 'true' as it 'accords with the laws of that world.'

title: The Subcreation Theory of J.R.R. Tolkien (Mirante)
rule: Secondary belief needs rigorous inner consistency, joined to an accurate view of the primary world. The reader's belief, not the author's invention count, is the measure.
example: 'You therefore believe it, while you are, as it were, inside.'

title: How to Make an Apple Pie: Ecologies and Economies in SFF (Reactor; Jenn Lyons)
rule: Follow consequences bottom-up: terrain and climate, then ecology, then economy, then politics. Ask staple crops, herd animals, predators; trade follows what the land can support; resources drive conflict; check how food is processed, not just named; do not import potatoes or tomatoes by default. Consistency of how changes link matters more than realism. Everyday objects should be made of what the world has.
example: Apples are an expensive import in her city of Ompher; sugar was once a spice in medieval Europe; removing horses changes warfare, trade and disease; Europe has no hyenas because wolves took the niche.

title: systemic worldbuilding (agent skill, via search summary)
rule: Staged consequence tracing: first order (who gains, what is obsolete), second (new markets, shifts in value, power), third (language, taboos, belief). Ask where value and scarcity come from; trade without supply chains is a common failure. Low-reliability source, a skill listing.

title: Shadow of the Torturer & Claw of the Conciliator (SF Book Club page)
read: full (via fetch summarizer; one page, low depth)
rule: Wolfe's technique: archaic or obscure words that are real, never invented, used for things of a far-future world. The reader gets a riddle with a lookup, not a coinage; the strangeness has a dictionary behind it. The page names Lexicon Urthus (Andre-Driussi) as the reference.
example: fuligin ('the colour that is darker than black', from fuliginous), optimates, aquastor, fiacre. Claim that Wolfe drew words from English-Latin or English-Greek dictionaries is from a low-quality page, unverified.

title: The Dying Earth: An Appreciation (Black Gate)
rule: Vance voice: formal, ornate syntax turned by a 'but'; dry, ironic narration that mirrors characters hiding brutality in elaborate speech; wit from timing and implication, not vocabulary alone (compared with Wodehouse). The dying world arrives through lost history and tossed-off catalogued detail ('Who, this far away in time, can recall?'), not exposition.
example: 'Willingly will I aid you,' said Pandelume (then a 'but'); coined words intercongeles, suprapullulation, crystorrhoid; the Excellent Prismatic Spray; opening: 'a red sun wearily makes its way through the skies of Earth and the moon is no more.'

title: Gormenghast review (Deep Outside, via search summary)
rule: Peake names fit the person's role or temperament (Steerpike, Sepulchrave, Swelter, Flay) and keep readers placed in one eccentric, Dickensian register; the prose builds mood by density, at the cost of slow reading. Reader impressions only; no scholarship on Peake's naming was found.
example: Sepulchrave, a melancholic whose only interest is his huge library; Steerpike, the self-advancing schemer.
